proposal.title: Is Newton–Muon's activation-covariance refresh worth its cost at tiny scale? A cost-accounted screen of a low-rank-plus-diagonal K inverse (likely revise/reject)
proposal.hypothesis: On a real-text tiny Transformer on MPS, replacing Newton–Muon's full damped inverse (K+γI)^{-1} with a rank-r eigen-plus-isotropic-remainder inverse, refreshed at the same interval, reaches a fixed held-out loss in at most 0.97× the synchronized wall-clock time of full-inverse Newton–Muon, with matched tuning.
proposal.baseline: Newton–Muon Algorithm 1 (2604.01472v1 chunk 0003). It keeps a per-layer EWMA K←βK+(1−β)ZZᵀ/N, refreshed every k steps. It sets γ_ℓ=γ·tr(K)/n and computes the inverse by float32 Cholesky with torch.cholesky_inverse. It right-multiplies the raw gradient as G K^{-1}, applied before momentum and the remaining Muon pipeline. MLP contraction uses a 4-block diagonal approximation. The source's default hyperparameters are β=0.95, γ=0.2 and k=32. No official code URL is supplied, which is a baseline-coverage gap. Muon itself (NS5) is the second required control.
proposal.operator_delta: At each refresh, replace the Cholesky inverse with a top-r eigendecomposition K≈VΛVᵀ plus an isotropic remainder ρ. The preconditioner becomes P=V[(Λ+γI)^{-1}−(ρ+γ)^{-1}I]Vᵀ+(ρ+γ)^{-1}I. It is applied as G·P, costing two n×r products per step instead of one n×n product.

contribution_claims.text: A cost-accounted, synchronized-timing tiny-scale screen of whether Newton–Muon's preconditioner overhead can be reduced without losing its time-to-loss benefit.
Low-rank-plus-isotropic inverse of the damped activation second moment. This is a known structured approximation that the source names as future work, not a new algorithm.
Hypothesized at most 3% time-to-loss gain over full-inverse Newton–Muon. This is unobserved.

mechanism_check.assumption_scope: Source-supported: ZZᵀ is strongly anisotropic in Pythia-70M, and moderate refresh intervals work best at 124M–455M on H100/L40S. Inferred target assumptions: the spectrum of K in a tiny model is concentrated enough for small r, and inverse cost is a material fraction of step time on MPS. A tiny model is an untested regime, not a contradiction of the source results.
mechanism_check.specialized_operation: Algorithm steps: 1) Update K as in the baseline. 2) Every k steps, run an r-step subspace iteration or eigh on K to obtain V and Λ. 3) Set ρ to the mean of the remaining eigenvalues, (tr K − ΣΛ)/(n−r). 4) Each step, compute G·P = (G·V)·D·Vᵀ + c·G, where D is the diagonal correction and c=(ρ+γ)^{-1}. 5) Pass the result to the standard Muon pipeline. If r=n, P equals (K+γI)^{-1} exactly. If r=0, P=cI, which is Muon up to a scale that msgn removes.
mechanism_check.remaining_effect: The only surviving effect is the cost reduction from O(n³/k + mn²) to O(nr²+ … + mnr) at a reduced fidelity. At n≤512 the per-step G·K^{-1} matmul is small relative to forward/backward, so the saving may be negligible. Whether it is negligible is the unresolved question.
mechanism_check.simplest_baseline: Full-inverse Newton–Muon with a larger refresh interval k. Its known limitation is staleness. Plain Muon, which adds zero overhead, is the floor control.
mechanism_check.distinguishing_test: Cheap analytic and operator test first. Measure the fraction f of synchronized step time spent on refresh plus preconditioning in full Newton–Muon on MPS. Cost/benefit rule: proceed to training only if f>5% and the rank-r P keeps a quadratic score s(Q) of at least 0.9× the full inverse on held-out batches. Even then, the quadratic score is not accepted as evidence of better training.

evidence.supports: The exact inverse method used by the baseline.
The proposed delta is source-named future work.
The benefit margin is small, so overhead matters.

assumptions: The overhead fraction f is above 5% on MPS for d≤512.
The top-r eigenvalues capture most of the preconditioning effect.
Speedups reported at 124M–455M on H100/L40S do not transfer to this setting and are not assumed to.

data_paths.input: Training-batch activations Z and gradients G
data_paths.operation: EWMA K, rank-r eigendecomposition, right preconditioning
data_paths.possible_leakage: None from held-out data. The held-out split is used only for loss evaluation at fixed intervals.

proposal.counterexample: At small n, the full Cholesky inverse every 32 steps costs under 1% of step time. Then no time saving is possible, and any approximation can only lose quality.
proposal.matched_control: Full-inverse Newton–Muon with identical β, γ, k, learning rate, seeds, data order and NS steps. Only the inverse operator differs. Plain Muon is included as a floor control.

experiment.development: Fresh small real-text corpus split, about 6-layer d=256–512 Transformer, 3 seeds, learning-rate sweep matched across all methods.
experiment.heldout: A different untouched text domain with a d=512 model, a fresh seed set, and no reuse of old fixtures.
experiment.metric: torch.mps.synchronize-timed wall-clock to a fixed held-out loss, median over seeds. Peak optimizer memory is also reported.
experiment.kill_threshold: Reject if f<5%, or if the quadratic-score ratio is below 0.9. Also reject if median time-to-loss is not at least 3% better than both controls with no seed worse than full Newton–Muon by more than 2%. Note that Newton–Muon itself may fail to beat Muon at this scale, which also ends the project.

proposal.prior_art_difference: Newton–Muon already uses block-diagonal approximations and suggests low-rank factorizations and polynomial inverses. Appendix F's negative results concern Σ_W, not K. The only difference here is the specific rank-r-plus-isotropic inverse together with a strict cost audit. It is not established as new, and there is no matching local experiment. Muon2-F, CacheMuon, HiMuon, Polar Switch and the spectrum-adaptive NS work target the orthogonalization step, not this component, and their full details are unverified.
